newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Dictators get support in Latin America - poll.
newsitem.headline: Dictators get support in Latin America - poll.

text.p: A poll released on Friday shows more than a third of Latin Americans either openly support the return of authoritarian rule or are indifferent as to whether they live in a democracy or not.

The Latinobarometro (Latinbarometer) 1996 survey, carried out simultaneously in 17 countries across the continent and in Spain, shows 17 percent of the Latin Americans polled would support the return of an authoritarian regime and another 17 percent said they were indifferent to the form of government.
The numbers contrast sharply with results from Spain where only eight percent said they would approve the return of authoritarian rule and seven percent said were indifferent.

"Our conclusion is that while most people support democracy, that support is not as high as in established democracies such as Spain," organisers of the poll said in a statement. They said they saw the high degree of "indifference to the governing regime" as a protest against democracy.

The Latinobarometro 1996 poll, the first ever Latin American survey of its kind, interviewed 21,198 people in the 18 countries using urban samples of an average of 1,200 people in every country. The poll, sponsored by the European Union and using a methodology developed by Eurobarometer, surveyed views on democracy, the economy and regional integration.

Democracy remains a relatively new phenomenon in Latin America, where over the last 15 years more than a dozen countries replaced authoritarian and military-sponsored dictatorships with democratically elected governments.

The poll showed 80 percent of those surveyed believed much needed to be accomplished before achieving full democracy. That feeling was particularly high in Brazil and Colombia where more than 90 percent of those polled expressed a desire for more democracy.

But 72 percent said they would be willing to defend their democratic government if its survival were threatened. That percentage was very high in Bolivia and Ecuador but significantly lower in Chile where just 53 percent said they would be willing to fight for democracy.

Professor Bolivar Lamounier of the IDESP political research institute, the Brazilian co-ordinator of the poll, said perhaps the most alarming message from the survey was the strong association between democracy and economic well-being.

"Clearly the population's satisfaction with democracy is very dependent on the government's economic success," said Lamounier, adding the popular perception was that only the elites had benefitted from the transition to democracy.
"This is a sign that we still have a long way to go," Lamounier said.

Despite the success of most Latin American governments in bringing down inflation and putting their economies back on track, a vast majority of those polled believed Latin America was a poorer continent than in the past.
Sixty-nine percent of those polled in South America and Mexico said their countries were poorer while just 19 percent of Spaniards polled said poverty was worse.

With inflation mostly under control, people in South America and Mexico rated unemployment and education as their country's top economic priorities. Those polled in Central America said inflation and unemployment were the most serious problems faced by their governments.
